\section[scadere]{scadere — to expire, to run out; to fall due}

\label{lesson:IT-C388-scadere}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Italian for to exclude, then the Italian for the condition.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: scadere}
\textbf{scadere} — \textquotedblleft{}to expire, to run out; to fall due\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Il mio passaporto scade a marzo.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{My passport expires in March.}
\end{quote}

Conjugated like \emph{cadere}, with \emph{essere}: \emph{è scaduto}. Of food, \emph{scaduto} means past its date.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{scadere} is built from \emph{s-}, from Latin \emph{ex-}, and \emph{cadere} \textquotedblleft{}to fall\textquotedblright{}, inherited from Latin \emph{cadere} (Lewis \& Short): the date falls due.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{scadere}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{scadere}, once more
  \item \emph{Say it:} a sentence of your own with \emph{scadere}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Italian for to exclude, then the Italian for the condition, then say \emph{scadere} again
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does scadere mean? (\textquotedblleft{}To expire, to run out; to fall due\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[valido]{valido — valid; worthwhile, sound}

\label{lesson:IT-C388-valido}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Italian for the condition, then the Italian for to expire.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: valido}
\textbf{valido} — \textquotedblleft{}valid; worthwhile, sound\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Il biglietto è valido per una settimana.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{The ticket is valid for a week.}
\end{quote}

Of an idea or a person: \emph{un valido motivo} — a sound reason.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{valido} is a learned borrowing from Latin \emph{validus} \textquotedblleft{}strong, effective\textquotedblright{} (Lewis \& Short), from \emph{valēre} \textquotedblleft{}to be strong, to be worth\textquotedblright{}.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright

  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{valido}, once more
  \item \emph{Say it:} a sentence of your own with \emph{valido}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Italian for the condition, then the Italian for to expire, then say \emph{valido} again
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]

\section[rinnovare]{rinnovare — to renew}

\label{lesson:IT-C388-rinnovare}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Italian for to expire, then the Italian for valid.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: rinnovare}
\textbf{rinnovare} — \textquotedblleft{}to renew\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Se non rinnovi la carta, non puoi prendere libri in biblioteca.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{If you do not renew the card, you cannot borrow books from the library.}
\end{quote}

\emph{Rinnovare la casa} — to do up the house.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{rinnovare} comes from Latin \emph{renovāre} \textquotedblleft{}to renew, to make new again\textquotedblright{} (Lewis \& Short), built from \emph{re-} and \emph{novus} \textquotedblleft{}new\textquotedblright{}.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}

  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Italian for to expire, then the Italian for valid, then say \emph{rinnovare} again

\section[il rinnovo]{il rinnovo — the renewal}

\label{lesson:IT-C388-rinnovo}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Italian for valid, then the Italian for to renew.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: il rinnovo}
\textbf{il rinnovo} — \textquotedblleft{}the renewal\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Per il rinnovo serve una foto nuova.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{For the renewal you need a new photo.}
\end{quote}

Built on \emph{rinnovare}. \emph{Il rinnovo del contratto} — the contract renewal.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{rinnovo} is built on \emph{rinnovare} \textquotedblleft{}to renew\textquotedblright{}, from Latin \emph{renovāre} \textquotedblleft{}to make new again\textquotedblright{} (Lewis \& Short), on \emph{novus} \textquotedblleft{}new\textquotedblright{}.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.

\section[la tessera]{la tessera — the card, the membership card, the pass}

\label{lesson:IT-C388-tessera}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Italian for to renew, then the Italian for the renewal.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: la tessera}
\textbf{la tessera} — \textquotedblleft{}the card, the membership card, the pass\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Con la tessera del museo entri gratis.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{With the museum card you get in free.}
\end{quote}

Stress on the first syllable: \emph{tèssera}. For buses, a monthly pass.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{tessera} is a learned borrowing from Latin \emph{tessera} \textquotedblleft{}a square tablet, a token, a ticket\textquotedblright{} (Lewis \& Short), which goes back to Greek \emph{tésseres} \textquotedblleft{}four\textquotedblright{}, for its four corners.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}
